comment: The equity principle is strong on geographic, connectivity and institutional constraints, but it does not address user-side capability constraints. Across the life course, people may experience changes in vision, hearing, dexterity, cognition, language, literacy and digital confidence. Unless these are treated as architectural concerns, a service may be technically available yet practically unusable. ITU-T F.780.2 already recognises accessibility requirements for telehealth services, including older persons with age-related disabilities.

citation.raw: §1.4 — VII. Equity and Inclusion p.44 l.325–343

public.text: The equity principle is strong on geographic, connectivity and institutional constraints, but it does not address user-side capability constraints. Across the life course, people may experience changes in vision, hearing, dexterity, cognition, language, literacy and digital confidence. Unless these are treated as architectural concerns, a service may be technically available yet practically unusable. ITU-T F.780.2 already recognises accessibility requirements for telehealth services, including older persons with age-related disabilities.
public.suggestedRevision: Add after line 343: “Equity and inclusion also require the architecture to accommodate variation in functional ability, disability, language, literacy and digital capability across the life course. Countries should require age-inclusive and accessible interaction patterns, multimodal channels, low-complexity workflows and assisted-access pathways, so that participation in DPI-H does not depend on independent use of a smartphone or any single digital channel."
